pages.alt: Arrow A, 3 long, and arrow B, 4 long, laid tip to tail and turned 397° together. The sum arrow is 5 long, and the bars stack A's height, 1.8, and B's, 3.2, to the sum's, 5.
pages.name: Two arrows, one sum
pages.text: Here are two turning arrows, like From circle to wave's arm. Arrow A is 3 long and points right; arrow B is 4 long and starts a quarter turn on. B's tail sits on A's tip, [[tip to tail]], and a bold arrow runs from the centre to B's tip: the [[sum arrow]]. Pause it, or drag A's tip.

pages.alt: Arrow A, 3 long, pointing right, and arrow B, 4 long, a quarter turn on, laid tip to tail at the start, with the waves of A and B over two turns and the sum wave, peaking at 5.
pages.name: The sum's peak
pages.task: A is 3 long pointing right, and B is 4 long a quarter turn on. How high does the sum wave peak?
pages.why: A and B are at right angles, so the sum arrow is the long side of a right-angled triangle: `√(3² + 4²) = √25 = 5`. The sum wave's peak is the sum arrow's length. 7 adds the lengths, which works only when the arrows point the same way, and 1 takes one from the other, which works only when they point opposite ways.

pages.text: Now A is 10 long, pointing right, and B is 6 long at 60°. To measure the sum, split each arrow as in Finding angles: its [[floor shadow]] is its length × cos of its angle, and its [[wall shadow]] its length × sin. B's are `6 cos 60° = 3` and `6 sin 60° = 5.196`; A lies on the floor, so its wall shadow is 0. Slide B and watch the shadows follow.

pages.task: A is 4 long pointing right, and B is 4 long at 60°, tip to tail. How long is the sum arrow?
pages.why: Split B: floor `4 cos 60° = 2`, wall `4 sin 60° = 3.464`. The floor shadows add to `4 + 2 = 6` and the wall shadows to 3.464, so the sum is `√(6² + 3.464²) = √48 = 6.93`. 8 adds the lengths as if the arrows lay in a line. 4 uses the cosine rule with 60°, but inside the tip-to-tail triangle the angle is `180° − 60° = 120°`.

pages.task: The same arrows: A 4 long pointing right, B 4 long at 60°. At what angle does the sum arrow point?
pages.why: The sum's floor shadow is 6 and its wall shadow 3.464, so its angle is `tan⁻¹(3.464 ÷ 6) = 30°`, halfway between A and B because they are the same length. 60° is B's own angle, and 0.577 is `3.464 ÷ 6`, the tan of the angle, before taking tan⁻¹.

pages.alt: Arrow A, 10 long, and arrow B turned half a turn, from 60° to 240°, laid on its tip. The arrow from the centre is A − B, 8.72 long at −36.6°, and its wave is A's wave minus B's.
pages.name: Taking a wave away
pages.text: To take B away from A, turn B's arrow half a turn and add it. An arrow half a turn on has every height with its sign changed, so its wave is B's wave upside down. Here B turns from 60° to 240°. The floor shadows give `10 − 3 = 7` and the wall shadows `0 − 5.196 = −5.196`, so A − B is `√(7² + 5.196²) = 8.72` long, at `tan⁻¹(−5.196 ÷ 7) = −36.6°`, below the floor. Switch it off to add B instead.

pages.text: A three-phase supply has three voltages, L1, L2 and L3, equal in size and 120° apart, with L2 a third of a turn behind L1. In the UK each is 230 V rms between phase and neutral, so this card is drawn at rms. Each line's voltage is measured from neutral, so a meter across L1 and L2 reads one minus the other, L1 − L2: turn L2 half a turn and add it to L1.

pages.task: A meter across L1 and L2 reads the arrow joining their tips. Each phase is 230 V, and they are 120° apart. What does it read?
pages.why: The meter reads L1 − L2. Turn L2 half a turn and add it to L1: floor `230 + 115 = 345`, wall 199.2, so `√(345² + 199.2²) = 398` V, which is `230 × √3`. 460 V adds the two sizes, which happens only when the phases are half a turn apart, and 230 V is one phase's own arrow, measured to neutral.

pages.alt: Arrow A, 3 long, and arrow B, 4 long, laid tip to tail, with B turning twice for each turn of A. The sum arrow is 5 long at this moment, and its length keeps changing.
pages.name: Twice as fast
pages.text: One phasor diagram works only for waves of one frequency. Here B turns twice for each turn of A. Now the angle between them keeps changing, so the tip-to-tail triangle changes shape: the sum arrow stretches and shrinks as it turns, and its wave is no longer one clean sine wave. The heights still stack at every moment, but no single steady arrow stands for the sum. Switch B back to A's speed and the shape holds.

pages.alt: Arrow A, 3 long, and arrow B, 4 long, with B turning twice for each turn of A, shown an eighth of a turn in. The waves of A and B are drawn, and the sum wave, which is not one sine wave.
pages.name: B twice as fast
pages.task: B now turns twice for each turn of A. What does the sum arrow do?
pages.why: B gains a whole turn on A every turn, so the angle between them keeps changing. The tip-to-tail triangle changes shape, and the sum arrow runs from `4 − 3 = 1` to `3 + 4 = 7` long. Its wave repeats, but it is not one sine wave, so no single phasor stands for it.

pages.task: A college's marine notes say most ships have a three-phase 440 V supply: 440 V between lines. What is each phase-to-neutral voltage?
pages.why: Line voltage is phase voltage × √3, so phase voltage is line voltage ÷ √3: `440 ÷ 1.732 = 254` V. Halving treats the phases as half a turn apart, and `440 × √3 = 762` goes the wrong way, from phase to line.

pages.alt: Arrow A, 8 long, pointing right, and arrow B, 8 long, half a turn on, laid on A's tip so it points straight back to the centre. The waves of A and B are mirror images, and the sum wave is flat at 0.
pages.name: Opposite arrows
pages.task: What is the peak of `8 sin ωt + 8 sin(ωt + 180°)`?
pages.why: B starts half a turn on from A, so laid tip to tail it points straight back, and its tip returns to the centre. The sum arrow has no length, so the waves cancel at every instant: the sum is 0. 16 adds the lengths, as if they pointed the same way, and 11.3 is `√(8² + 8²)`, as if they were a quarter turn apart.

pages.task: Two branch currents join: 12 A peak in step with the supply, and 5 A peak a quarter turn behind it. What is the supply current?
pages.why: Lay the 5 A arrow, a quarter turn behind and so pointing down, on the tip of the 12 A arrow. The floor shadows give 12 and the wall shadows `0 − 5 = −5`, so the sum is `√(12² + 5²) = 13` A at `tan⁻¹(−5 ÷ 12) = −22.6°`: below the floor, lagging. 17 A adds the sizes, and leading drops the minus sign of the wall shadow. Later, complex numbers write an arrow's floor shadow and wall shadow as one number, so adding phasors becomes adding numbers.
